full_text:
This blog by Nick Hillman OBE, HEPI’s CEO, is based on a speech delivered to senior managers and governors at the University of Winchester.

I began my career as a History teacher, then passed through Whitehall as a higher education policy wonk before alighting at HEPI. Along the way, I have served as a governor of multiple education institutions, including infant and secondary schools and two universities as well as the Slough-based National Foundation for Educational Research. The schools and universities that I have served as a governor have experienced some fearsomely successful collaborations – the University of Manchester, for example, resulted from the merger of UMIST and the Victoria University of Manchester over 20 years ago. Today, I am the governor of an independent school that has built up a family of 11 schools around the world and also of a local grammar school that is part of a multi-academy trust that already includes six schools.

Successful institutional partnerships are not easy, neither pre-ordained nor guaranteed. That is why, in a recent HEPI Policy Note, I argued that institutions need multiple jigsaw pieces to be in place to succeed in transnational education, including:

entrepreneurial leaders with spare bandwith;

trusted in-country partners;

access to capital;

a global reputation for quality;

a clear understanding of, and a plan to deal with, cultural differences;

an ability to weather storms and conflicts;

an educational ethos that is transferable to another jurisdiction; and

patience.

Despite such hurdles, the variable geography in place across our university system is continuing to change at pace – in contrast, perhaps, to public perceptions of higher education as a slow-moving beast.

Recent and current initiatives include:

the merger of the University of Greenwich and the University of Kent into LASE (the London and South East University Group);

the tie-up between Cranfield University and King’s College London;

a new local ‘strategic alliance’ between Scotland’s Rural College, Queen Margaret University and Edinburgh Napier University;

various joint initiatives for new medical schools, including the Pears Cumbria School of Medicine between Imperial College London and the University of Cumbria and the Black Country Medical School partnership between the University of Wolverhampton and Aston Medical School;

the purchase of Lincoln Bishop University by Global University Systems, a multi-national for-profit chain; and

the London Interdisciplinary School joining emlyon [sic] Business School as part of an ‘ambition to build a Global Management & Tech University.’

On the other hand, the history of UK higher education is littered with examples of mergers and collaborations that did not get far off the drawing board. Examples from England include attempted university tie-ups in the south between Solent and Southampton, in the Midlands between Birmingham and Nottingham and in the north between Lancaster and Liverpool.

I know of one former Cabinet Minister who used to ask in private why no British county had yet copied the state-by-state model seen in the United States. A truly regional university that brought together different institutions with different campuses boasting different strengths is surely not beyond the realm of possibility, even if the journey towards it remains quite hard to map in practice.

Other initiatives, including some transnational projects by UK universities and UK schools, have flopped too, costing millions of pounds and doing little to spread education while creating an opportunity cost and various headaches back at base. Meanwhile, questions have been asked about the extensive franchise arrangements made by a range of newer universities.

So institutions scoping out options for future partnerships need to tread carefully. To help think this through, I want to focus on the main alternative approaches on offer, based on two sources that seem to contradict one another. Both are based on what is happening in the United States, where they are ahead of us in redrawing the provision of higher education.

Big is beautiful

The first approach is summed up by the old idea that ‘big is beautiful’. It is outlined in the HEPI / Ellucian Policy Note, Risk and Resilience: What UK higher education can learn from the United States, written by Dr Dan Greenstein, formerly the Chancellor of Pennsylvania’s State System of Higher Education among other high-profile roles.

Dr Greenstein’s lessons from the US are all about the importance of building revenue. His paper begins by arguing that, in the US higher education sector, where something like 800 institutions have closed in just six years, two variables alone have determined success and failure:

The first is whether … [public support for teaching] holds its value – that is, it is indexed to inflation. The second is whether the institution can respond by raising its price, recruiting more students, or changing the credentials it offers.

Let’s take those points in turn. In England, tuition fees and loans for home undergraduates have not held their value since the Coalition Government introduced £9,000 fees back in 2012 (and despite the current inflation-linked rises).

Recruiting more students was nonetheless an option for most institutions in the years afterwards, thanks to the removal of student number caps in the mid-2010s and a more liberal migration system in the early 2020s.

Expanding recruitment is, however, no longer so easy for most institutions: high-tariff universities have sucked up more of the available UK applicants while tougher migration rules have made recruitment from overseas harder. The percentage of school leavers enrolling in higher education is flat or falling and a substantial reduction in the number of 18-year-olds is hoving into view (and has just arrived in Scotland).

Dr Greenstein notes UK universities have (even) less room for manoeuvre than US institutions:

They carry private-sector exposure at public-sector speed.

So he concludes revenue matters above all else:

Every American case of an institution or system pulling out of a deteriorating trajectory involved it acting on revenue, not costs alone. … That is why the American systems that went furthest in consolidating their operations, sharing back-office functions across their campuses more comprehensively than anyone else in the data, are also among the most financially distressed. They executed. The execution was real, and technically impressive. It never touched the variable driving the decline.

On this argument, recovery has to come from increasing revenue: austerity bolsters efficiency but does not deliver growth. This could be said to imply financially distressed institutions should undertake franchising and transnational education at scale, and also seek to make the most of the new opportunities offered by England’s incoming Lifelong Learning Entitlement too.

This is the strategy followed by some UK universities. As Tom Richmond wrote in a recent HEPI report:

BPP University saw its student numbers increase by 421 per cent from 2015/16 to 2024/25, the University of Law increased by 1,811 per cent and Arden University increased by 3,217 per cent. Meanwhile, Regent College London, a smaller provider, expanded by 1,408 per cent (from 510 to 7,180 students). Canterbury Christ Church University appears to have achieved its stunning growth from 12,450 to 34,655 students (+278 per cent) through franchising partnerships, as did Buckinghamshire New University and Bath Spa University …

Market obsessed

But another piece of evidence from the United States, a book called Capitalizing on College: How higher education went from mission driven to market obsessed by Joshua Travis Brown, appears to hold different lessons. It looks at various case studies of US higher education institutions which have expanded their enrolments in four different ways. All four strategies sought to build revenue. But the problem is none of them worked.

The first route focused on increasing traditional residential enrolments. Yet the institutions following this path found they had to offer discounts to fill their spaces and, in the end, their previous financial challenges returned. As I recounted in my review of his book, Joshua Travis Brown argues that, except at the very top of the tree, ‘tradition cannot compete in the market.’

The second route focused on taking higher education to the learners, whether in shopping malls, conference hotels or even military bases. This initially worked but delivered quality concerns and competition wiped out the early benefits:

enrolments cratered, and the excess revenues … evaporated.

The third approach, focused on new markets such as transnational education. But excessive complexity and rising costs meant the early benefits eventually disappeared.

The final approach of selling mass online education led the institution in question to lose touch with its original values.

These two conflicting pictures are based on actual experiences: one suggests growth in student numbers is the only sensible strategy for a hard-pressed institution; the other suggests this will come back to bite you on the bum.

The risks of franchising, for example, include cannibalising existing campus provision and, besides, Ministers are gunning for franchising at the moment. Transnational education is, in contrast, the flavour of the month in Whitehall, as it seems to allow an increase in educational exports without directly impacting on the migration numbers. But it is very hard to do well and profitably – by which I mean delivering a comparable experience to those at the mothership institution – even for large, old and prestigious universities with deep pockets.

Where to go next?

There are nonetheless two areas where more growth might be easier to find. The first is the Lifelong Learning Entitlement. Demand for this is uncertain and it could yet prove to be the dampest of damp squibs but it is being built on top of existing systems and will not entail institutions having to do anything half as complicated as building a new campus abroad or climbing in bed with a franchisee that risks a hard-fought reputation. Is the Lifelong Learning Entitlement, therefore, a route to new and expanded markets for individual institutions operating on their own or in collaboration with other providers and employers?

The second is investigating the scope for reaching further into those sections of society that remain hugely underserved by higher education. We still have an official target from Keir Starmer’s day of getting two-thirds of people through some form of higher education. Yet we all know that higher education participation varies significantly by age. It also varies significantly by socio-economic status. And by sex: 10 years after we hit Tony Blair’s target of 50% participation in higher education by those aged under 30, we are still nowhere near hitting it for boys.

So we should not entirely take our eye off more traditional activity. If we as a sector were to play our hand right, then it is not even completely inevitable that a reduction in 18-year-olds much mean a reduction in students. (It didn’t in the 1990s.)

title: College Living Cost Estimates Vary Widely
summary:
College Living Cost Estimates Vary Widely Joshua.Bay Tue, 10/20/2026 - 03:00 AM A new study of over 5,000 colleges finds wide disparities in how institutions estimate the cost of attendance, raising questions about affordability and financial aid. Byline(s) Joshua Bay College Living Cost Estimates Vary Widely
Joshua.Bay Tue, 10/20/2026 - 03:00 AM

A new study of over 5,000 colleges finds wide disparities in how institutions estimate the cost of attendance, raising questions about affordability and financial aid.

Byline(s)
Joshua Bay
full_text:
As students and families increasingly question the value of higher education, understanding the full cost of earning a college degree has become an important part of the affordability debate.

Federal law requires colleges to include estimated housing, food, transportation and other living expenses in their published cost of attendance, including for students living off campus. These allowances are generally estimates rather than carefully calculated charges from the institution, but they help determine financial aid limits and underpin measures such as net price and unmet need.

New research released today by the Hildreth Institute compared the published living-cost allowances at 5,235 colleges against consistent external benchmarks based on local housing, food, transportation and other expenses. It found that colleges serving students in the same local markets often publish markedly different living-cost estimates, making it harder for students and families to compare college costs and assess affordability.

Bahar Akman Imboden, managing director at the Hildreth Institute, said inaccurate or inconsistent living-cost estimates can have implications beyond students’ initial college decisions, potentially affecting their access to financial aid and ability to cover essential expenses.

“Colleges aspire to appear affordable,” said Akman Imboden. “College affordability cannot just be measured on whether students perceive college to be affordable at the time of entry. It must also account for whether that student has the resources to persist and complete.”

Uneven living-cost estimates: The research includes three reports—a primer, an analysis of living-cost estimates and an examination of standardization—as well as an interactive dashboard that explains how colleges develop living-cost estimates, how they compare with local costs and how institutions coordinate their approaches.

The analysis examined two reported categories: food and housing, and “other expenses,” which includes transportation and miscellaneous personal costs. It focused on full-time, first-time undergraduates living off campus, but not with family.

Beyond the estimates: Akman Imboden said part of the challenge of developing accurate living-cost estimates is that financial aid administrators are required to create a standard budget, often with limited guidance and resources, for students whose circumstances can vary considerably.

“Two colleges may have access to the same actual accurate local data on rentals, but one assumes two students share a two-bedroom apartment, while the other assumes four students share the same kind of two-bedroom apartment,” Akman Imboden said. “This results in housing allowances that can be dramatically different, and of course, that’s assuming that financial officers have easy access to such data.”

Akman Imboden noted that unexpected expenses and unmet basic needs can create serious barriers to persistence and completion. Although the study does not directly measure those outcomes, she said it raises questions about what happens when the living-cost allowances students use to plan for college do not reflect the expenses they ultimately face.

“There is a very legitimate concern there that higher-cost living allowance could make an institution appear less affordable and potentially discourage enrollment,” she added. “A budget that is too modest can make a college appear more affordable … so a student may enroll, even take out a loan based on this initial picture, only to discover that their actual expenses are beyond their means.”

“If those financial pressures prevent students from completing, then we risk the most troubling kind of outcome of higher education, which is debt without a degree,” she added.

Jeremy Thompson, research director at the Hildreth Institute, said colleges are not generally required by the federal government to publicly explain how they calculate individual components of their cost of attendance estimates. While some institutions and systems publish their methodologies, many do not, making it difficult to understand what drives differences between colleges.

He pointed to the study’s geographic findings, which showed that colleges in smaller towns and rural areas tended to report food and housing allowances above the benchmark but estimates for other expenses below it.

“It’s possible that a concentrated student population in a rural area with relatively scarce housing is competing for a limited supply of housing close to campus,” Thompson said. “But we need more transparency to understand how schools are calculating it to really drill down on what accounts for that difference.”

Toward greater consistency: Approaches to coordinating and standardizing cost of attendance estimates vary considerably by state. In Colorado, statewide budget parameters help reduce variation but may not fully reflect differences in local costs, according to the study. California uses shared survey data and different system-level approaches, including centralized methodologies that produce campus-specific budgets.

Louisiana has voluntary model budgets developed by the state financial aid administrators’ association, while the City University of New York system uses centrally determined budgets informed by local cost data.

At a time of heightened concern about college affordability and public trust, the findings underscore the importance of clearer and more comparable cost information. The report notes that the FAFSA Simplification Act restored the U.S. Department of Education’s authority to regulate most cost of attendance components beyond tuition and fees, creating an opportunity to consider what should be standardized across colleges and what should remain responsive to local costs and individual circumstances.

Thompson said the goal should be to standardize the methodologies colleges use rather than require institutions to report identical living-cost estimates.

“If you put out there a standard set of assumptions that schools are expected to use, and then issue some suggestions for how to factor in adjustments, then you create flexibility within a consistent framework,” Thompson said.

Akman Imboden emphasized that even with more consistent methodologies, institutions must account for the different financial circumstances of the students they serve.

“One budget cannot fit every student, and at the minimum, we owe students a clear explanation of what that budget assumes and a meaningful way to address the circumstances it does not capture,” she said. “If we are really serious about improving student success, we need to understand the financial realities of the students we actually serve.”

title: Education Affordability a Priority for Voters
summary:
Education Affordability a Priority for Voters Katherine Knott Tue, 10/20/2026 - 03:00 AM In a new survey from Jobs for the Future, policies aimed at lowering education costs received overwhelming bipartisan support. Byline(s) Katherine Knott Education Affordability a Priority for Voters
Katherine Knott Tue, 10/20/2026 - 03:00 AM

In a new survey from Jobs for the Future, policies aimed at lowering education costs received overwhelming bipartisan support.

Byline(s)
Katherine Knott
full_text:
Affordability concerns are top of mind for registered voters ahead of this year’s midterm elections, and that extends to education costs, according to a new survey from Jobs for the Future, a nonprofit focused on the intersection of education and the workforce.

Just 43 percent of the 2,000 registered voters surveyed said they had enough money to enroll in a college degree program, and 66 percent said they would be more likely to support a candidate who focused on making education and training more affordable, according to the results released today and shared exclusively with Inside Higher Ed.

Jobs for the Future partnered with Morning Consult on the survey of registered voters conducted in late September. The survey highlights some key concerns and priorities for voters in the midterm elections, which will determine which party controls Congress for the rest of President Trump’s term in office.

Over all, nearly 60 percent of respondents said the economy is on the wrong track and 53 percent felt economically secure. Responses varied according to political affiliation and geography. About 20 percent of independents surveyed said the economy was headed in the right direction, compared to 58 percent of Republicans.

Independent voters were also more likely to say they felt economically insecure and that they have a bright economic future. Rural voters showed more pessimism about the economy compared to urban voters.

“Voters are heading to the polls with one issue at the top of their minds: the economy, and what it means for their own paychecks and prospects,” JFF President Maria Flynn said in a news release. “Independents in particular are telling us they don’t feel economically secure and don’t see enough candidates talking about how to solve their most pressing needs. In an increasingly volatile economy, quality jobs and affordable pathways to get them are kitchen-table issues, and the candidates who speak to them have a real opportunity to earn voters’ trust.”

Proposals to address affordability at the federal level received overwhelming bipartisan support from the respondents, according to a summary of the results. That includes making dual enrollment low or no cost, preserving need-based financial aid and giving students credit for prior learning and work experiences.

About 36 percent of voters surveyed who didn’t have a four-year degree said they could afford to pay for college. Among those who were unemployed, 29 percent said they had enough money to pay for college. Slightly more people in both groups said they could afford a nondegree program.

Karishma Merchant, vice president of policy and advocacy at JFF, said in the release that the survey results show that whoever wins in November will have a mandate to act on policies that could make education and training more affordable.

“Voters across the political spectrum are asking for the same thing: a fair shot at a good job and an affordable way to get the skills to land one,” Merchant said. “Apprenticeships, work-based learning, and financial aid for short-term training draw support from roughly three in four voters in every party.”

title: From Iran to AI: the six key voter issues shaping the US midterm elections
summary:
Much of Donald Trump’s unpopularity in polls stems from dissatisfaction over the economy and war on Iran

  • US politics live – latest updates

full_text:
Next month’s midterm elections will test Donald Trump’s second term and determine whether Democrats regain political power in Washington. Polls show Trump’s approval ratings at their lowest across his two presidencies, pulled down by widespread economic dissatisfaction and an unpopular war against Iran. Here are the key issues shaping this year’s elections.

The economy

Despite Trump’s 2024 campaign pledge to tackle affordability issues, the economy consistently ranks as voters’ top concern. A recent Associated Press-NORC survey showed only 26% of voters approving of Trump’s handling of the economy, two percentage points below Joe Biden’s worst ratings on the issue.

Iran

Trump’s decision to go to war with the Tehran regime has exacerbated economic worries. Iran’s retaliatory decision to close the strait of Hormuz has driven up gasoline prices for US motorists.

It also represents a breach of his pledge to end the US’s supposed addiction to “forever wars”. Democrats and some Republicans also complain that he embarked on military action without congressional authorization.

Immigration

Enforcement and closing the border remains a signature issue for Trump. He repeatedly boasts of the impact of his closure of the southern border as one of his biggest achievements, making comparisons with the performance of Joe Biden.

But the mood has since shifted. High profile violent incidents involving Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) and Customs and Border Protection agents have fed a perception that the immigration crackdown has “gone too far”.

Trump’s power

The president is not on the ballot, but has told voters to pretend that he is. His visibility makes his character and exercise of power a central issue at a time of career-low approval ratings and a swirl of controversies over corruption allegations and his various pet building projects.

Democrats have framed the midterms as an opportunity to rein in the president.

Artificial intelligence and datacenters

AI has emerged as a key campaign issue, with surveys showing a majority of voters holding negative views on it, even as Trump champions its development and attempts to rename it “super intelligence”.

Up to 70% of Americans oppose the construction of AI datacenters in their areas, polls show.

title: Australian democracy is usually peaceful. But there’s a homegrown history of political violence | Joshua Black and Frank Bongiorno

The alleged attack on independent MP Helen Haines in Wangaratta has shocked a nation whose politics is normally peaceful even by the standards of mature democracies. A hard-working, decent parliamentarian with a strong moral compass and a gift for achieving consensus, Haines seems an especially unlikely figure to attract the kind of brutality allegedly visited on her on Monday.

We do not yet know the motivation behind this alleged attack. But there is no question Australia’s politics have been fractious over the past 12 months. Violence, literal and rhetorical, has been a growing feature of the landscape, shaping the relations between citizens and politicians – and among one another. The Bondi beach massacre of 14 December 2025 is widely regarded as a tragic turning point in this regard.

But like other features of our public landscape, both good and bad, political violence has a history in Australia – one from which we may learn.

Australian assassinations

Australian leaders have mostly avoided the assassinations more common in other places. Even Australia’s parent culture, Great Britain, lost a prime minister to an assassination in 1812 when John Bellingham shot Spencer Perceval through the heart in the lobby of the House of Commons.

The 20th century alone saw two sitting American presidents murdered, along with leading activists and major aspirants to higher office. Two Indian prime ministers, Indira Gandhi and her son and successor Rajiv Gandhi, were slain in the century’s later decades, as well as an Israeli statesman in Yitzhak Rabin.

No Australian prime ministers or premiers have been assassinated to date. The deaths of figures such as Joseph Lyons, John Curtin and Ben Chifley were the result of natural causes. The circumstances of Liberal prime minister Harold Holt’s death are well known but, notwithstanding conspiracy theories, did not involve foul play.

Still, assassination attempts have occasionally blighted Australia’s political landscape. The first came in 1868 with the visit of Prince Alfred, second in line to Queen Victoria’s throne. The prince was shot at a welcome event near Sydney by an Irish republican with evidence of mental illness.

The assailant was executed, but the prince lived, saved by the bullet hitting a metal clip of his trouser braces. The attempt set off a new wave of sectarian animosity between Protestants and Catholics, ably stoked by Federation father Henry Parkes. (There was much less fuss after the apparent attempt on the life of then-Prince Charles in Sydney in 1994, though in that case the bullets were blanks.)

In the 1960s, it was war and peace that stirred political passions. Labor leader Arthur Calwell was an opponent of Australia’s involvement in the Vietnam war, and it was after a “rowdy meeting” about conscription in Sydney in 1966 that he was shot in the jaw by Peter Kocan, who had a leaning to far-right politics and was evidently ill.

Calwell forgave Kocan, who became a writer of some renown.

Crime and corruption were also potential motivators of assassination. In July 1977, anti-drug campaigner and Liberal candidate from Griffith in the Riverina, Donald Mackay, went missing. His vehicle was found stained with blood, but his body was never recovered. His presumed death precipitated a state royal commission into drug trafficking.

In 1994, John Newman – Labor’s New South Wales state MP for Cabramatta and a committed opponent of criminal gangs – was murdered in his driveway. Fairfield councillor Phuong Ngo, a local notoriety with a party power base and criminal links, was later convicted, though with many questions left unanswered.

Political violence

While assassinations have been rare, political violence has at times made its mark on Australia. The spearing of governor Arthur Phillip in the right shoulder in September 1790 was an early instance, though as Kate Fullagar explains, this incident was likely a payback ritual orchestrated by Yiyura man Bennelong in the hope of enabling detente rather than committing murder.

In the early 19th century, political violence centred on frontier conflict and warfare between settlers and Indigenous communities. The University of Newcastle’s massacre map remains a telling window into that world.

Democracy itself was, at times, a violent thing. The goldminers’ rebellion at Eureka in 1854 – triggered by unhappiness with licence fees and colonial administration generally – left more than two dozen dead, most of them miners or civilians. Miners also violently attacked Chinese diggers at Buckland River in Victoria (1857), with some fatalities, and Lambing Flat in NSW (1861).

The prospect of similar violence hung in the air during the industrial strikes of the 1890s. Colonial troops in Melbourne were ordered to “fire low” on union agitators and “lay them out”. In western Queensland, soldiers intimidated striking shearers with Nordenfelt machine guns.

Historian Sean Scalmer has shown that early colonial elections were marred by violence and even occasional killings on the hustings. Australia’s unique history of electoral innovation, including the secret ballot and broad suffrage, was partly an attempt to “contain contention”, as he puts it.

There was growing violence in Australian politics – and society – from the 1960s. Anti-war protests occasionally erupted into conflict. On a few occasions, so did the demonstrations against Sir John Kerr, who had dismissed the Whitlam government in November 1975. These involved various projectiles including, in one instance, a brick to smash open a window of the vice-regal car.

Party struggles also contained an underbelly of factional violence. In 1980, leftwing Labor activist Peter Baldwin was bashed in Sydney, the instigators presumed to be rightwing opponents. It was an extreme case, but factional battles in Liberal party branches in Sydney have occasionally descended into fisticuffs in the more recent past, too.

The 1980s and 1990s saw several massacres in suburbs such as Sydney’s Milperra (1984) and Melbourne’s Clifton Hill (1987). Some, including Milperra, were precipitated by gang wars, but the ready availability of guns was of broader concern to many, including senior Liberal John Howard.

He was prime minister by the time he went to the regional Victorian town of Sale, where he was explaining his controversial gun law reforms and firearm buyback program. The measures were a response to the devastating Port Arthur massacre in Tasmania. Howard famously wore a bullet-proof vest to the lectern, an instruction from his security personnel but an apparent insult to his audience.

Terror on southern shores

The late 20th century was also an era of growing terrorism in Australia. Croatian extremists and Yugoslav agents were seemingly at war with one another in the streets of Melbourne and Sydney.

In the latter city, a deadly attack on a gathering of world leaders at a regional Commonwealth heads of government meeting occurred in 1978. The likely suspects, an Indian religious sect-turned-cult, appear to have targeted the Indian prime minister, who was meeting with Malcolm Fraser and other leaders at the Hilton hotel. Multiple innocent bystanders, including two unlucky garbagemen who accidentally picked up a bomb left in a bin, were killed.

There was also suspected terrorism at play when, in December 1980, an assassin’s bullets killed the Turkish consul-general Şarık Arıyak and his bodyguard outside the former’s Sydney residence. Armenian activists claimed responsibility for the murder, but evidence was lacking. Today, the NSW police reward for information stands at $1m.

Prime ministers and other senior politicians have sometimes been rumoured to be the targets of terrorists. Yet there was always risk of hoaxes. A supposed plan by a Sri Lankan PhD student to assassinate Malcolm Turnbull and Julie Bishop, and target major Sydney landmarks, was revealed to be fabricated. The conspirator, a colleague of the accused, was later jailed over forged evidence.

Threats to democracy

Political officeholders are increasingly at risk of political violence around the world, and not only in autocratic settings where physical coercion is a regular political tool. In the past decade, British parliamentarians Jo Cox and Sir David Amess were killed in office, and more recently the former MP Ann Widdecombe was brutally killed in her own home.

In 2022, the assassination of former Japanese prime minister Shinzo Abe in Nara by a man with religious grievances shocked the world. So had the storming of the US Capitol a year earlier. In that case, a violent mob threatened to assassinate congressional leaders along with the sitting vice-president, Mike Pence.

Such scenes at the heart of the United States, which historically thought itself a democratic beacon for the world, were astonishing. People forgot it was also the product of a revolutionary political culture.

There are some common causes for concern. The internet and social media have made it easier for angry or unwell people to threaten politicians’ safety. On Monday night, Australia’s home affairs minister Tony Burke said there were 1,067 reports of “harassing and threatening behaviour against various high office holders” in the last financial year alone.

Turning the temperature down

While we still don’t know if the alleged attack on Helen Haines was politically motivated, condemnation of the incident has united politicians of different stripes. Haines is a much-admired figure across the parliament. Responding to the alleged attack, the prime minister, Anthony Albanese, called for the political “temperature to be turned down”.

Democracy is a practice as much as a system. It requires for its survival a steady nurturing by those – citizens as well as representatives – who perform it. Haines herself has been in the forefront of efforts to restore trust in a political system that has generated disaffection among many Australians in recent years. She has been repaid with a violence that is the polar opposite of all that she stands for.

Australia’s world-leading history of electoral innovation was partly an effort to mitigate against violence. But the innovations of an earlier generation may not be enough to defend democracy from today’s threats, not least those arising from a social media ecosystem that draws its oxygen from base emotions.

Resting on the laurels of compulsory and preferential voting is not an option. Sober reflection from political participants – in practice, everybody – is what our present circumstances demand.

title: The AI doom scenario you've never heard of may be hardest to stop
summary: The time to prepare for "gradual disempowerment" is now, according to researchers. One calls it "a civilization-scale problem."
full_text:
It seems that almost daily, a big tech company releases a new AI-driven digital assistant. Muse by Meta, Gemini by Google, dots by OpenAI. By the time this article is published, a new one from [insert tech company here] will probably have a press release touting its ability to manage your work and life — to take things off your plate, automate your processes, speed up your tedious tasks. It sounds helpful and, to lower the bar, harmless.

But some researchers say this is the beginning of a treacherous path for humankind, one where bots take more and more off our plate until all that's left is an empty vessel, and we human users become nothing more than thoughtless "approvers."

It's not just a threat to jobs. They warn that allowing our skills and knowledge to deteriorate, and surrendering our critical thinking to AI, poses an existential danger to humanity.

One term for this path is "gradual disempowerment" — a scenario where AI displaces human labor in the economy, replaces human decision-making in all key societal concerns, erodes human creativity, and degrades human cognition along the way.

And though the word "gradual" is in the name, that does not mean the problem is something to worry about far in the future, according to experts.

"I put gradual disempowerment on the very top of my list," said Jay Chooi, the founder and CEO of Robocurve, a company that tracks and measures AI-driven robotics capabilities.

Chooi believes gradual disempowerment is just as worrisome as the threat of engineered pandemics and more destructive cyberattacks, which could be accelerated by capable AI.

"It's a civilization-scale problem," Chooi said of gradual disempowerment. "A lot of people feel very powerless, because it requires a lot of effort and a whole-of-society approach to solve it."

What is "gradual disempowerment" and how could AI cause it?

The term "gradual disempowerment" stems from a paper published in early 2025.

At the heart of the gradual disempowerment scenario is AI technology continuing to advance in capabilities, as it has rapidly since the launch of ChatGPT in 2022.

AI models may soon be better at nearly all cognitive tasks than humans — solving frontier math problems, doing hard science, coding, writing and creating art and music, to name a few of the areas where AI increasingly excels. At the same time, advances in robotics could lead to AI-powered robots performing better than humans at physical labor like packing boxes, constructing homes, building cars, painting murals, mining for rare minerals, and even building IKEA furniture.

We like to think that in an ideal world, the best applicant generally gets the job, and they are paid based on the level of demand for their skills. But imagine if a human is never the best person for the job. That's a world that some AI prognosticators and whistleblowers expect.

It's a world where an AI agent or AI-enabled robot is better at every task and sub-task that it takes to do my job and your job. They move faster than us, think deeper, have more patience and stamina. They more cordially answer phones, do more thorough research, and more dexterously wield a scalpel or a nail file. Plus, they never need to sleep or take sick days, they never show up hungover or moody, and they never threaten to leave for a better job.

To picture gradual disempowerment more clearly, here's a scenario: Let's say you run Hammer Co., a company that manufactures hammers. You have line workers who shape the steel heads and wooden handles and then fit them together, and managers who keep the factory running smoothly. You have people who maintain your supply chain and teams to handle marketing, sales, accounting, and all the other functions that help your business thrive.

But then a tech company comes out with AI-powered Hammer Bots. The robot workers can make hammers far faster than your human workers, while AI agents can run the business side with little oversight. They'll work all night, never make mistakes, and cost far less than your happy, well-paid staff. You don't want to fire your human workers. You see them around town and have known their families for years, after all.

But your competitor gets the Hammer Bots. Most customers just want the cheapest hammers — they don't care who or what makes them. As CEO of Hammer Co. you either compete or die. So you fire all your humans and get Hammer Bots to replace them.

Now, try to envision this is the case for every company, and every job. With normal free-market incentives, the company that stays loyal to its human employees will be outcompeted by the company that gets AI to do the work instead.

Here's where gradual disempowerment comes into play.

The fewer humans that participate in labor, and the more work that's outsourced to AI agents, the more humanity becomes dependent on AI for decision-making and the more human skills deteriorate. How long until the finer points of hammer-making will be forgotten?

With AI making all our complex decisions for us, humans become less capable of understanding and overseeing those decisions or of pushing back against them.

"If people aren't actually practicing the skills that the agents are doing for them, they lose the ability to have that skill, and so now you become reliant," said Margaret Mitchell, an AI research scientist at Hugging Face and co-author of another recent paper on the importance of keeping humans in the loop in an AI world.

"What happens when something goes wrong? There's no human you can point to who can fix it. So now you've become fully dependent on these systems to fix themselves, and what if that's not possible?"

A risk to democratic governance

It's not just economics and labor at risk. Take the military, for example. All or most decisions in war involve humans today, even if AI contributes to the process, but the balance is likely to shift as the technology becomes more capable.

If the United States uses AI to make decisions in battle, its enemies across the field will be pressured to do the same. The side that leans more heavily on humans will be slower and less efficient. Human soldiers need food and rest. Robot soldiers will not. Human decision-makers are limited in the scenarios they can conceive and plan for; AIs can take into account all of human knowledge.

"The states need citizens. They need us because we pay taxes and we fight for the states in the military," said Jan Kulveit, a co-author of the gradual disempowerment paper and co-founder of ACS Research Group.

States also use people to enforce laws. But what if law enforcement is all automated in the future?

"If, or when, existing states don't need their citizens, they're less likely to be democratic," said Kulveit.

Kulveit compares theoretical future countries that are mostly run by AI to oil states today. He said the oil states tend to be authoritarian because they don't rely on most of their citizens to pay taxes and don't need citizens' votes to rule. States that rely on AI to run the economy and military could have similar outcomes, said Kulveit.

If that is the case, and citizens no longer are the backbone of labor or warfare in a world of gradual disempowerment, then humans lose perhaps their greatest leverage against those in power.

"A lot of people are talking about rogue AI hacking into data centers and taking over the world, but it is not in the mainstream consciousness that like AI could literally take over the world just by continuing to do what it's supposed to do, which is automating everything," said Jay Chooi of Robocurve.

"Organizations are all going to have a very strong economic pressure, and political pressure, to phase out humans and move work more and more into robots or AI."

How does humanity avoid gradual disempowerment?

Humans ceding control to AI, say the gradual disempowerment authors, is almost a natural transition once very advanced AI is here.

Gradual disempowerment "does not need to emerge from a deliberate scheme or powergrab by AI systems," wrote Kulveit and his colleagues. "In the short-term, it is being incentivized by the perceived value that AI systems can bring to economic, cultural and state functions."

"We can't be in the situation where we are competing with the machines," said Kulveit. "Because if we are just competing with the machines, we will probably lose."

The gradual disempowerment authors believe stopping our disempowerment may be a heavy lift for humanity, since it involves complex systems that feed into each other — government, culture, and the economy.

"This may be a bigger challenge than merely preventing AI systems from pursuing overtly harmful goals," they write.

One first step in slowing disempowerment is keeping indicators of how much work is being ceded to AI, and of what kind of specific jobs AI systems are capable of handling. If thousands of workers are being displaced by AI in, say, call center jobs, it helps to know that in granular detail.

But measurement isn't enough without action, Mitchell said. She argues that removing humans from the loop in AI processes both worsens oversight and degrades the skills of the human overseer. Therefore, companies and leadership in all fields must take proactive steps to keep humans engaged.

"This general practice within tech is we want our systems to be frictionless," said Mitchell, referring to the idea that everything should move fast and without obstacles. "There's this sense that the less friction the better, but there's been a push within the more ethical AI community that strategic friction can be good because it can draw people's attention to critical issues that otherwise they might overlook."

Mitchell argues that strategic friction — keeping humans in the work loop at predetermined steps — can be done both by developers of AI, companies like OpenAI and Anthropic and Google, and by companies and organizations that deploy AI. Thoughtful and purposeful design of AI can benefit society as a whole, and the individuals who use it.

Kulveit agrees that AI should be thoughtfully designed to add value to humans, not necessarily replace our every task.

"You want to carve out places where we agree that we will not allow competitive pressures to remove humans from the loop," he said. "It would be nice if the companies train the AIs to be more complementary to humans. Currently, the AIs are implicitly trained to be a replacement for humans. But you can imagine training the AIs so they are better at explaining to us what's happening."

Kulveit is describing AI that doesn't just spew out the answers to whatever question you ask it, at the very least in sectors where it is critical to include human expertise and decision-making, like war. Quick and easy answers can be helpful, but they can also make you dependent and credulous, believing anything the chatbot tells you, whether right or wrong.

But AI can be more than that. It can help you not just by doing the work for you, but by educating you along the way. That way the human worker continues to learn while using AI as a partner, not a substitute.

"There has been such a singular focus on capability or functionality of these systems to the detriment of people, to the detriment of users," said Mitchell. "If your only goal is to get a high score on a benchmark, then you are not going to be taking into account cognitive support design. But if your goal is to make a system that works really well for people — like if the race is for a utility as opposed to benchmark score — then you end up designing fundamentally different systems."

If gradual disempowerment really is a large-scale risk, compared to more talked-about doom scenarios — like AI helping to design bioweapons or chemical weapons — it may suffer from a relative lack of vividness.

"We know what it means for a robot to take over the world. We know what it means for countries to nuke each other," said Chooi. "AI taking over the world is very legible in the human consciousness. But gradual disempowerment? No one has made a movie about gradual disempowerment."

But to Chooi, gradual disempowerment is very easy to picture.

"All the organizations have the incentives to adopt it and phase out humans," he said. "This is a very logical conclusion. It's not very hard to see it."

title: Can the new federal voucher program help public schools? Democrats are torn
summary: The new scholarship tax credit program could help public school families pay for some educational services, but advocates worry it could do more harm than good.
full_text:
Catch up on what you missed with our Education newsletter, sent weekly.

Democrats and public school advocates have until the end of the year to make a tough decision: Whether to embrace a Republican program that might help some public-school families pay for things like tutoring and summer school – even if it will also pour taxpayer dollars into private schools.

Colorado's Jared Polis was the first Democratic governor to opt in to the coming Federal Scholarship Tax Credit, a new program the Trump administration is calling "America's first nationwide school choice program."

"An obvious decision," says Polis of his choice to embrace the policy that, with the help of a generous tax credit, could raise billions of dollars in taxpayer donations nationwide.

"Of course I want Colorado kids to be the beneficiaries of that," Polis tells NPR. "I think many other governors would like kids in their state to be the beneficiaries of that."

Many Republicans, yes. But his fellow Democrats aren't so sure.

"That is never going to happen," Minnesota Gov. Tim Walz said earlier this year when asked if he would be opting his state into the program for 2027. "We are not doing it."

In between Polis and Walz, between yes and no, 15 Democratic governors, as well as the mayor of Washington, D.C., remain undecided, according to a tracker by Ed Week. And the clock is ticking. To be able to participate next year, they have to opt in by Jan. 1.

"This is really, really hard because the policy is designed to try to make these [political] wedges," says Jessica Levin, litigation director at Education Law Center, a nonprofit legal advocacy group that opposes private school vouchers.

She says Democratic governors may feel they can't pass on this program "because they think, 'Oh, there is a benefit for public schools, and I'm going to get flack.'"

But Levin, along with many of her fellow public school advocates, sees the program as a kind of Trojan horse. Billed as a boon to public schools, she says vouchers can lead some families to leave for private schools, which can then result in declines in public school funding.

How the tax credit will work

Beginning in January, qualifying taxpayers will be able to donate up to $1,700 to a scholarship-granting organization, or SGO. The SGO will then convert those donations into scholarships, also known as vouchers, to help families cover a wide range of education costs, including private school tuition as well as tutoring, summer school and even new computers.

The government's end of the bargain is that, in exchange for making a scholarship donation, these qualifying donors will get every penny back come tax season: For every dollar they contribute to one of these SGOs, they will owe the IRS a dollar less in federal income tax up to $1,700.

Put another way, if you're thinking of donating, "It's not your money. It's money that you would have sent to the IRS," says Marguerite Roza of Georgetown University's Edunomics Lab.

More than 138 million people could qualify for the full tax credit, according to the Institute on Taxation and Economic Policy. Plus, given the generosity of the credit, the U.S. Treasury Department predicts it could raise nearly $26 billion in scholarship donations by 2030.

For comparison, the largest source of federal education funding, known as Title I, sent more than $18 billion to schools in 2023 to help them serve low-income students.

Of the 31 states that have signed on to the new program, most are led by Republicans. Just one Democratic governor has willingly joined Polis: Gov. Kathy Hochul of New York. In Kansas, Kentucky and North Carolina, top Democrats fought the program but were overridden by Republican legislatures.

If a governor does not opt in, that state's taxpayers can still make donations to SGOs and receive the tax credit, but families in that state won't qualify for scholarships or vouchers to pay for educational expenses.

Governors who have opted in for 2027 can also choose to opt out for 2028 or vice versa.

Why some opponents feel they need to get on board

Like many of the nation's Democratic governors, groups that have championed public education in Republican-led states now face a similarly uncomfortable choice:

Continue to fight the scholarship program on principle or make a practical pivot, encouraging school districts and public school families to embrace the program so they can benefit from it.

The Southern Education Foundation (SEF) – created in the aftermath of the Civil War to guarantee schooling to the children of formerly enslaved people – chose to pivot.

"The question for me became less about whether I agreed with every aspect of the program, because I don't, and more about what happens now that the program is moving forward," Raymond C. Pierce, SEF's president and CEO, saidin a press release.

"We've always been an organization that has promoted public schools, and we oppose private school vouchers," says Fred Jones Jr., SEF's senior director of public policy and advocacy.

Jones says foundation leaders fought "very hard" against the new program but decided to change their approach after most of the states where they operate opted in. The group is now launching an alliance of SGOs to focus specifically on raising funds for public school students.

"If we have tutoring, if we have afterschool programming, if we get summer learning… I think a number of students in the public school system could be tremendously better off," Jones says.

Deborah Gist felt the same way. "I am making sure that public school students benefit," she says.

The former superintendent of Tulsa Public Schools, one of Oklahoma's largest districts, Gist recently founded Future School Fund, a national SGO focused on serving public school students.

"I pulled up the bill language itself and saw right there that public schools were very explicitly included," Gist says. "So I immediately started wearing my public school educator hat. I immediately started thinking about all the kinds of things that we could fund."

Even with help from organizations like SEF and Future School Fund, public schools in states that have opted-in will have a lot of catching-up to do.

Many states already have state-level tax credits focused on helping families pay for private school, and very few of the SGOs that are already up and running are public school-oriented.

In other words, Jessica Levin explains, private schools already have the SGOs, the infrastructure and the advertising budgets.

That's one reason Levin, along with many other public school advocates, continues to push back against the tax credit. She predicts, "The vast majority of the money is going to be used on private school tuition and other private education expenses."

To get the money, public schools will need to start charging fees

Marguerite Roza says public schools hoping to benefit from the tax credit will now need to decide which of the services they provide might legally be reimbursed.

"You can't charge a fee for math class," Roza says, or for much of what public schools do.

At its most basic, the program allows families to use donations to pay for education services that they'd normally have to cover out of pocket. That's a challenge for public schools, since they are required to provide education free-of-charge — they can't start charging for traditional services just so they can receive donation dollars through the new tax credit.

Private schools, on the other hand, can legally charge tuition, and the Republican program can easily be used to reimburse families for that cost. What can public schools charge for?

Roza has some ideas. "A fee could cover field trips, assemblies, access to tutoring, access to aftercare, homework drop-in hours, end of the year parties."

That doesn't sit right with Levin, though. She says, even if this kind of reimbursement is allowable under the law, "it's very wrong and very dangerous. Public schools don't charge for most of what they provide because that's the entire point of public education."

The best way to support public schools, she says, "is to fund public schools. It is not to accept a privatization program that throws a few crumbs at public school students."

When it comes to generating money for public schools, Roza agrees this new tax credit is "the most convoluted, circuitous way possible anybody could have ever laid out — and with all sorts of caveats in it."

But, she says, it's also a real program that won't benefit districts unless they actively embrace it.

For the tax credit to raise a meaningful amount of money for public school communities, Roza says, they will not only need to team up with public-school focused SGOs. They'll also need to convince local employers to include the option to donate as part of their regular payroll operations. School districts will want to fold it into their own payroll systems.

"The money is not showing up automatically," Roza says. "Districts will have to play this game in order to get the money. And where districts shrug their shoulders and say, 'I'm not doing this, I'm not gonna participate,' then they're not going to get any."

Wealthier public schools will have a big advantage

Even if some public school communities do everything right, and money pours in, an old problem is sure to surface: The schools that need the most help, may benefit the least.

"It's the public schools that are in wealthy communities that have the most money locally that they can raise," says Jon Valant, senior fellow at the Brookings Institution and director of its Brown Center on Education Policy. "And if the patterns of giving for this program look like patterns of giving for other programs across the country, we expect that most people are going to give to [SGOs] that then give back to the schools in their communities."

Valant and a team of Brookings researchers estimate that the wealthiest counties will generate roughly three times as much money through the program as the nation's poorest counties.

And that means, for lower-income, rural communities to benefit, they'll have to rely on wealthy donors' willingness to give beyond their own communities. That's not likely, Valant says.

What's more, the program is not limited to helping low-income families.

A student can qualify for help as long as their household earns less than 300% of the gross median income in their area. That's roughly 95% of all students, according to the Treasury Department's own estimates. Valant says, "There are kids across the country whose families make a half-million dollars a year who are income-eligible."

Given how disproportionately the program is likely to benefit wealthy communities, Valant warns, "there's a real chance that we end up seeing this program as Title I for rich kids."

All of which makes the decision to opt in or out that much harder for hold-out Democrats.

For Fred Jones Jr., of SEF, embracing the program was purely practical. He doesn't like it, and would advise those undecided Democratic governors to opt out. But, in the South, where SEF works, most states have opted in. It's real, like it or not.

title: How the Trump administration's crackdown on international students could affect the economy
summary: A new proposed $70,000 fee for international students who are seeking to work in the U.S. after graduation is the latest Trump administration policy targeting scholars from abroad.
full_text:
The administration has additionally increased fees and restrictions for H-1B employment visas that international students often rely on to continue living in the U.S. years after graduation.

"The goal seems to be to shrink the foreign-born population in the U.S.," said Tara Watson, senior fellow of economic studies at the Brookings Institution.

These policies, several of which have been halted by courts, signal a departure from Trump's repeated assurances that he is pro legal immigration, and from his campaign promise to grant international students permanent residency after graduating from U.S. colleges.

READ MORE: Trump said he's pro legal immigration, his policies say otherwise

The restrictive policies have had detrimental effects on international students and universities, experts told PBS News.

A preliminary analysis by NAFSA in August estimated a drop in international student enrollment by 111,000 in 2026, which would result in up to $3.4 billion in lost revenue.

Here's what to know about the Trump administration's policies targeting international students, the effect the potential changes are expected to have and how they compare to other countries.

Why is Trump targeting international students and foreign workers?

The Trump administration has given an array of reasons for its policies targeting international students and workers.

In its proposed rule published on Oct. 8, the Department of Homeland Security said requiring universities to pay $70,000 per international student to participate in Optional Practical Training (OPT), a program that lets foreign students temporarily work in the U.S. after graduation, was necessary to "place the United States' interests first and protect American workers."

The administration gave a similar justification for its proposed rule to impose a filing fee exceeding $100,000 for companies to hire highly skilled workers on H1-B visas and to suspend certain tech companies from using the program altogether.

WATCH: Vance says Microsoft is being suspended from green card program for H-1B visa workers

The administration also cited fraud and abuse in its justification for the rules increasing fees for international students and workers.

DHS did the same in a July rule requiring student visas to be awarded for a fixed four-year period rather than until students complete their programs. A federal judge temporarily blocked the rule before it went into effect.

The administration has also cited national security and the country's best interest in its restrictions, including a State Department mandate to vet applicants' social media accounts.

In January, the State Department announced on X that it had revoked 8,000 student visas "for individuals who had encounters with U.S. law enforcement for criminal activity."

For months, international students reported receiving notices that their visas had been revoked without being given a reason. Many visas have been restored following court challenges.

READ MORE: International students stripped of legal status in the U.S. are piling up wins in court

At the time, Secretary of State Marco Rubio said his department was revoking visas from people who were acting against the U.S. national interest, including by protesting Israel's war in Gaza. However, the Associated Press reported that many of the students affected by the revocations didn't fit that description or had minor infractions.

Why does the U.S. rely on international students and workers?

Historically, the U.S. has been considered a "preeminent destination for the world's best and brightest," Aw said.

Watson described a "pipeline by which we take a really talented, highly educated group of people, and we bring them into our labor force."

The route begins with international students getting their undergraduate or more advanced degrees at universities and then working for one year or longer under the OPT program, depending on their field of study. U.S. companies then sponsor highly skilled workers' H1-B visas and eventually those employees may go on to become permanent residents and U.S. citizens.

Most of the more than 1 million international students in the U.S. pay full tuition at colleges and universities, which in turn helps subsidize American students' education, said Ted Mitchell, president of the American Council on Education.

He disagreed with the administration's argument that international students take opportunities away from U.S. citizens.

READ MORE: Trump says skilled foreign workers take jobs away from Americans. It's not that simple, experts say

"Higher education in America lives in a world of abundant opportunities," Mitchell said. "There are more spaces in colleges and universities than there are students, there are more opportunities for researchers and professors than there are applicants."

International students and workers make crucial contributions to the U.S. economy, experts told PBS News.

A 2023 study published in the National Bureau of Economic Research found high-skilled immigrants play an outsized role in innovation in the U.S. via the creation of patents.

"It's fair to say that global talent is a taproot of innovation in the United States," said Michael Clemens, economics professor at Johns Hopkins University.

International students who don't stay in the country after graduation can also help the U.S., Mitchell said. Those students may go on to hold positions of power in their home countries.

"They're the best kind of soft power that we have," Mitchell said. "Inculcating American values in people who return to leadership positions in their country."

What will happen if there is a drop in international students and workers?

The effects of Trump's policy decisions will partly depend on how long the policies remain in place and whether the system returns to the way it used to be, experts told PBS News. However, they agreed that deterring skilled international students and workers from coming to the U.S. will negatively affect the economy down the road.

"I worry that as we compress the number of people that are coming in through that pipeline, we're really going to see results in 10 or 20 years that our workforce will no longer be the place for the world's best and brightest to be working," Watson said.

Clemens said the main effects will take years to materialize, but will likely result in "fewer inventions, fewer new businesses and fewer new industries, at a time when we desperately need all of those things to adjust to the AI shock."

International students and workers also support the economy beyond their universities or workplaces. By living in the U.S., foreign students and workers create jobs as they buy goods and services, said Devashish Mitra, economics professor at Syracuse University.

How do Trump's proposals compare to other countries' approaches?

The administration's restrictive policies for international students and workers will lead people to choose countries other than the U.S. to pursue their studies, research and careers, according to the experts who spoke with PBS News.

"Students will not stop seeking places to study. Student mobility will continue," Aw said. "What is shifting is the direction and where they decide to study."

Mitchell said other countries that compete with the U.S. for talent and innovation see restrictive policies "as an opportunity to gain ground."

WATCH: Top researchers consider leaving U.S. amid funding cuts: 'The science world is ending'

China launched a new visa in 2025 intended to recruit young professionals in STEM fields.

Canada has hired researchers from U.S. universities amid the Trump administration's crackdown.

And the European Union created its "Choose Europe for Science" initiative in part to lure researchers from American universities.

"It is not inconceivable that new hubs of innovation could develop in other parts of the world," Watson said. "Because we're not leveraging this historic advantage that we've had."

title: Talent Beyond Borders: changing the narrative around international students – from tuition to talent
summary:
More must be done to change the public's perception of international students, says Edwin van Rest.

The post Talent Beyond Borders: changing the narrative around international students – from tuition to talent appeared first on The PIE News.
full_text:
Talent Beyond Borders started in late-night conversations with colleagues across the sector, including friends at Cambridge IELTS. And if I’m honest, it came from frustration, sometimes close to despair, around how international students are sometimes portrayed.

We really felt something needed to be done about the misinformation around and mischaracterisation of international students. Many of us have been international students ourselves and know they generally go on to create a lot of positive impact on the societies they touch.

But knowing this isn’t enough. We must show it. To do so, we need to win both hearts and minds, not only of policymakers but of the broader public.

Yet our own sector still talks about international education mostly as an “export”.

The most prominent reports from the big four destinations (the US, the UK, Canada and Australia) calculate students’ value from tuition, rent and local spending while they are studying. Add those four countries together and you get about $153 billion. Worldwide, the figure was last estimated at about $300bn.

However, that’s only the tip of the iceberg. As a sector, we have been seriously underselling ourselves. That’s why we launched Talent Beyond Borders – a research report that looks at the global economic and social impact of international graduates and the human stories behind them.

However, that’s only the tip of the iceberg. As a sector, we have been seriously underselling ourselves

Studyportals has the biggest data set of international enrolments in the world, and has been following students into graduation and their career. So we, together with Cambridge IELTS asked a different question: what do international graduates contribute to economies and societies once they start working?

Our numbers show that 41% stay in their country of study, 35% go home and 24% move on to a third country. Just the “stayers” from one graduating cohort, the class of 2024, will contribute an estimated $1.7tn to their host economies over their careers. Add the traditional figure and the total impact excedes $2tn. That’s roughly twice Switzerland’s annual GDP from one cohort. We’re no longer talking about billions. We’re talking about trillions.

And that’s before we count everything that’s harder to quantify: new businesses, trade links, skills gaps filled, soft power and classrooms that are richer for the mix of people in them. International graduates aren’t just an export. They are a real source of competitive advantage and have a positive impact on countries all over the world.

As Francesca Woodward, global managing director, English at Cambridge University Press & Assessment put it during the launch of Talent Beyond Borders: “International students bring significant cultural and social impact to countries all over the world. They enrich communities, plug vital skills gaps, boost diversity and help build stronger connections between people and countries”.

We know that in many leading economies, demographics are changing, and fewer and fewer young people are being born to fill tomorrow’s jobs. That’s why talent flows are inevitable, and they’ll only become more important in the decades ahead. I don’t believe countries that close their doors can stay as leading economies without attracting the right talent.

In the Netherlands, we saw significant anti-immigration rhetoric and serious discussion about forcing universities to increase Dutch-language undergraduate teaching to restrict international student flows.

At the same time, because of the talent narrative, the region introduced an initiative with large government support to attract more talent to the Netherlands to study and work in the semiconductor industry.

The government made €2.2bn available to strengthen the ecosystem and talent pipeline.

This shows that even within a populist political environment, universities can find a new way of demonstrating their relevance. For years we have been helping our universities to focus ‘beyond enrolment’: student success, graduation and now relevant employment.

It’s the idea of the fourth-generation university: an institution that doesn’t just teach and research, but helps build the regional economy around it, together with employers, government and talent drawn from all over the world. When employers add their voices, it creates a wider spectrum of social license for the sector.

Numbers persuade minds. To win hearts, though, international students also need a face. That’s the second part of Talent Beyond Borders: sharing their real, human stories. Where did they come from? What did their education mean to them? What career did they pursue and how do they contribute to society?

We’ll tell the stories of top CEOs, entrepreneurs and researchers, of course. But we’ll also tell the stories of teachers, nurses, carers and support staff, the people who keep our societies running, our kids and parents supported. In the same vision we also partnered with Made Impact to amplify stories demonstrating the everyday impact of international education.

We can’t do this alone. We need everybody in the sector to join us. And if we really want to reach our goals we need to get outside our echo chamber and connect with the general public, beyond our own bubble. The people we need to reach are policymakers, family dinner tables, community organisations and sports clubs.

So, please share your story, or the story of a remarkable international graduate you know and promote that everywhere, in particular outside our sector circle. When we help the world to more completely see the value of international students: we can enrich lives and connect our world.

Yes, we can change this narrative. Let’s do this.
