full_text:
Leadership Begins with the Heart

For 15 years, I tried to be the kind of school leader I would have wanted, which was one who met everyone’s needs all the time. I believed leadership begins with kindness. I believed it was essential to truly know people and to show up for them in a sincere, authentic way. I believed that if you gave your whole heart to a community, they would feel cared for and, in turn, do their best work for students and for one another, and with this leadership style in place, they did. I received positive feedback on a daily basis and I knew I was onto something. What I did not understand at the time was this: an open heart without boundaries slowly becomes an unsustainable one.

Naming a Philosophy of Care

In 2022, Rowman & Littlefield published The Heart of School Leadership (Stahl, 2022), a book I wrote based on my 15 years as a teacher and 15 years as school leader. In it, I organized my philosophy into 50 areas I believed were essential to effective leadership ranging from kindness and visibility to instructional leadership and equity. These areas were supported by research, specifically the Challenge to Care (Noddings, 2005), among others.

My book grew out of a deeply meaningful year when I served as a substitute principal in a large public elementary school. When that year ended, the faculty and staff gave me a red leather journal with a heart embossed on the front, filled with handwritten notes. It was more valuable than any title or salary I had earned. Those notes helped me unlock what I believed mattered most in leadership, and these ideals became the basis for my leadership book. This one was included in my preface:

‘Don’t cry because she is gone, smile because she was here.’ I heard this quote at a memorial service yesterday for a woman who died just nine days’ shy of her 101st birthday. She was described as an angel on earth—sweet, subdued, and endlessly patient. I knew her well–it was an apt description. Yet, when those words were spoken, it was you who sprang to mind. At one time or another, I have worked in every school, both public and private, in this district. Over the years, I have worked with more administrators than I can count. Happily, I have been able to work with all of them. So when you came to our school, I expected the experience to be the same. It was. Here is what I didn’t expect. I didn’t expect to find a person behind the desk who treated everyone equally, whose warmth was real, and whose joy was freely expressed and meant for all.’

After leaving school leadership to teach college full time, I began using my book in my graduate courses. At the end of each semester, I asked students to select three leadership areas and reflect on how they would influence their future practice. The discussions were powerful. This assignment also led to discussions about school culture, teaching philosophy, leadership style, and the effect of kindness and positivity in schools. Students affirmed the importance of relationships, positivity, visibility, and trust. I also believed I had modeled what I had written and the students confirmed this. Then something shifted.

When Students Redefined Care

When I presented my leadership framework at a professional conference, educators affirmed many of the relational traits I described. But they also raised questions I had not anticipated. Curious, I later sought IRB approval to more formally gather feedback from my graduate students. They weren’t yet working as teachers or leaders in the field so I was curious to see what they thought. It was an extra credit assignment where they rated the 50 categories as “important,” “somewhat important” or “not important” and added specific comments where they had feedback.

Similar to the conference attendees, the graduate students supported relational leadership, but not leadership that meant being everything to everyone. They spoke about sustainability. About balance. About protecting personal health and family life. They did not reject care-based leadership. They redefined it. Their feedback unsettled me on several levels and made me wonder if I had possibly modeled and written about unsustainable leadership?

When Devotion Becomes Depletion

For years, I had worn constant availability as a badge of honor. I answered calls while on vacation. I remember standing in Times Square, phone to my ear, listening to a teachers’ issue during spring break because it felt like what a committed leader would do, and I sincerely wanted to help. It’s who I am at my core. I was constantly available and responsive. I knew teachers’ children and dogs by name, and kept in touch with many after I left my last position. I attended every possible event. I was professionally available and often emotionally available, serving as part counselor as well as administrator. I believed this was devotion. In hindsight, I can see now that I had mistaken depletion for dedication.

There was also another layer to confront. I had worked alongside male leaders who practiced leadership differently and were far less visible and available than I was. Whether because of gendered expectations or my own internal standards, the responsibility to be endlessly visible and accessible fell primarily on me. It was fulfilling. It was meaningful. But in hindsight, it was also heavy.

Transition or Recovery?

When I transitioned into higher education, I experienced an quiet, unexpected loss of identity. I was no longer needed in the same urgent way. No one was calling during crises. No one required immediate decisions that only I could make. The teaching part came naturally, but I had also entered a world focused on research, publishing, and long-term scholarly contribution. It took me a while to understand this and I told myself I was simply in transition. It took some time to realize I was actually in recovery.

Over the next several years, I was offered multiple leadership positions and encouraged to return to school leadership. Each time, I felt a visceral resistance I could not fully explain. I had loved serving as a school leader and during my tenure I was honestly happy and energized. I am also someone who regularly follows directions and does what I am told, so in many ways as a leader I was responding to what people asked of me and needed, and above all following, “the Golden Rule.” After being away from leadership for a few years, something in me knew I could not return to that version of myself, and the graduate students’ feedback helped me understand why.

Sustainable Leadership for the Next Generation

Care-based leadership is essential. Schools are human institutions, and relationships matter deeply. But care that consumes the caregiver eventually undermines itself. Sustainable leadership requires boundaries, not as a retreat from responsibility, but as a protection of it. I still believe leadership begins with the heart. I still believe in knowing people, showing up, and building cultures of kindness, and I honestly wouldn’t change anything about my 15 years as a school leader because I am proud I gave so much. I believe I created a positive school culture. I now understand that I couldn’t have continued in that way, and that kindness must extend inward as well.

As I reflected on my last few years in higher education, I saw that I had begun replicating the same pattern with my college students and have been committed to constant responsiveness, extreme care and immediate availability. I think I did not recognize the toll it was beginning to take until I reviewed the responses from my study. I think that maybe I was looking for the same validation, and my student feedback conveyed I was giving my all, but if that were true, what was I actually teaching them as future educators?

The most meaningful lesson about leadership did not come from my years in administration or my own reflection after leaving it. It came from the graduate students who challenged my definition of care. They taught me that being everything to everyone is not the highest form of leadership. Sustainability is. To lead with your heart, you must also protect it.

Dr. Mary Louise Stahl is currently an Assistant Professor at Niagara University in New York and also an adjunct professor at the State University of New York at Fredonia. She earned her PhD in Educational Leadership in 2016 from the State University of New York at Buffalo, with her dissertation, “Chinese Students in United States High Schools.” She has worked for over 30 years in education, as a teacher, a school leader, a college professor and a writer. In 2022 Rowman & Littlefield published her book, the Heart of School Leadership.

References

Noddings, N. (2005). The challenge to care: An alternative approach to education. New York: Teachers College Press.

Stahl, M.L. (2002). The heart of school leadership. Rowman & Littlefield.

The Decimal Point Problem

During one of my first semesters teaching introductory biology labs at the college level, a student approached me after class visibly frustrated about a final grade. The difference between the student’s current average and the next letter grade was less than one percentage point. What struck me was not the disappointment itself, but how narrowly the conversation focused on decimals rather than learning. The student was not asking what concepts still needed improvement, which scientific skills needed development, or how to strengthen understanding moving forward. The discussion centered almost entirely on points.

Over time, I began noticing how frequently grading conversations in higher education become negotiations over mathematical precision. Students monitor learning management systems constantly, calculate hypothetical grade combinations, and focus intensely on small numerical differences that may not meaningfully represent actual differences in understanding. In many classrooms, grading can unintentionally shift attention away from learning and toward point accumulation.

This experience has made me reconsider how percentage-based grading systems shape student behavior in college courses.

When Students Chase Points Instead of Learning

American higher education relies heavily on highly granular grading systems. A student may earn an 89.4, a 91.7, or a 93.2, and those distinctions often carry emotional and academic significance. Yet as instructors, we should ask whether these fine numerical differences always represent truly distinct levels of mastery. In practice, many assessments contain unavoidable subjectivity, especially in written responses, projects, participation, discussion quality, or open-ended scientific reasoning tasks.

In contrast, many international grading models rely on broader performance bands such as 1–5 scales or competency-based descriptors. While these systems vary significantly across countries and institutions, they often place greater emphasis on overall mastery categories rather than hyper-precise numerical distinctions. The question is not whether one system is universally superior. Rather, the comparison raises an important instructional issue: How much grading precision is genuinely meaningful for student learning?

In my own courses, I have observed that highly detailed percentage systems can sometimes encourage transactional learning behaviors. Students may become preoccupied with recovering partial credit, calculating minimum scores needed for target grades, or strategically allocating effort based on point values rather than intellectual engagement. This does not mean students are unmotivated. In many cases, they are responding rationally to systems that reward optimization and numerical performance tracking.

At the same time, highly granular grading may unintentionally increase anxiety for students already navigating demanding academic workloads. Small numerical fluctuations can feel disproportionately important when students perceive every decimal point as carrying major consequences. In introductory STEM courses especially, where students may already experience high levels of performance pressure, grading structures can significantly shape classroom climate and motivation.

This does not necessarily mean instructors should eliminate percentage grades entirely. Many institutions require them, and numerical grading can provide useful feedback in certain contexts. However, college faculty can still take practical steps to reduce unhealthy fixation on points while keeping assessment rigorous and transparent.

As someone currently pursuing a doctoral degree while also teaching at both the secondary and postsecondary levels, I have found myself reflecting on grading from the student perspective as well. In several doctoral courses, I have received assignment grades reported with highly specific percentages even when the accompanying rubric used only whole-number performance categories. At times, this creates confusion about what the decimal-level distinctions are actually measuring. If a rubric category distinguishes performance broadly between levels such as “proficient” and “advanced,” the addition of highly granular percentages can give the impression of mathematical precision that may not fully align with the inherently interpretive nature of evaluating complex academic writing and analysis. More importantly, it can shift student attention toward trying to decode tiny numerical differences rather than focusing on substantive feedback, revision, and intellectual growth. As both an instructor and current student, these experiences have increasingly made me question whether highly detailed grading always improves clarity or whether it sometimes unintentionally amplifies anxiety and performance fixation instead.

Rethinking Feedback and Precision

One useful strategy involves shifting feedback emphasis toward mastery and growth rather than numerical outcomes alone. For example, when returning laboratory reports or written assignments, instructors can prioritize comments explaining conceptual strengths, scientific reasoning, and areas for improvement before students immediately focus on scores. Rubrics can also emphasize broader competency categories such as evidence use, analytical reasoning, communication clarity, or methodological understanding rather than excessively fragmented point breakdowns.

Another helpful approach is reducing unnecessary grading precision when appropriate. In some assignments, broader scoring bands may better reflect authentic performance differences than extremely narrow numerical distinctions. For example, distinguishing between “excellent,” “proficient,” “developing,” and “limited” scientific explanations may communicate learning quality more effectively than assigning a score of 87 versus 89.

Beyond Mathematical Accuracy

Transparency also matters. Students benefit when instructors explicitly explain what grades are intended to represent. Are grades measuring compliance, effort, conceptual understanding, skill development, improvement over time, or performance on isolated assessments? Many student frustrations emerge not simply from grades themselves, but from uncertainty about what those grades actually communicate.

I have also found that conversations about grading become more productive when students are encouraged to reflect on learning behaviors instead of solely final outcomes. Questions such as “What study strategies worked?” or “At what point did confusion begin?” often lead to more meaningful academic discussions than conversations focused entirely on whether one additional point can be recovered.

Grading systems shape more than transcripts. They influence motivation, classroom culture, student identity, and how learners define academic success. As higher education continues discussing student engagement, mental health, and authentic learning, grading practices deserve closer examination as part of that broader conversation. The goal is not to make courses easier or reduce standards. Rather, it is to consider whether our grading systems consistently direct student attention toward the forms of learning we actually value most.

Christopher Morales is a high school science teacher in Southwest Florida and an adjunct professor of biology at Florida SouthWestern State College. He holds both a bachelor’s and master’s degree in biology and is currently pursuing a doctorate in Educational Leadership at the American College of Education. His work focuses on student attention, learning environments, engagement, and instructional practice across secondary and postsecondary education.

title: Solving the experience Catch-22 for students
summary: The post Solving the experience Catch-22 for students appeared first on Advance HE UK.
full_text:
James McGarrigle, lecturer at North West Regional College, explores how meaningful industry experience can be embedded directly into the curriculum

Solving the Experience Catch-22 for Students

When I graduated with a First Class Honours degree, I expected it to open doors. I later completed an MSc with Distinction. Academically, I had done well, but when I tried to secure employment in my field, I repeatedly encountered the same problem: employers wanted industry experience.

It was a frustrating Catch-22: how do you gain industry experience if nobody gives you the opportunity to gain it?

Years later, as a lecturer, I began seeing students facing a similar challenge. They could develop knowledge, skills and strong portfolios, but the transition into professional practice could still be difficult without opportunities to apply their learning in real-world situations.

This challenge is also reflected in Alan Milburn’s Young People and Work: interim report, which highlights the importance of work experience and the barriers young people can face in accessing it.

Experience can be part of the curriculum

My own experience made me question how we could embed meaningful industry experience directly into the curriculum.

Not every student is immediately ready to work with an employer, and the level of support they need can change as their confidence and experience grow. This led me to think about how authentic learning can be scaffolded through different types of projects: starting with standalone projects, progressing to collaborative projects and, ideally, moving towards external live projects – with that scaffolding gradually reduced as students become more confident and independent.

“Industry experience doesn’t have to suddenly begin with a placement or first job. It can develop progressively through the curriculum.”

Importantly, I have found this doesn’t create more work for me as a lecturer. In collaborative projects, students from different curriculum areas and disciplines help drive the learning by working together, sharing their different skillsets while external partners help drive live projects through genuine briefs, feedback, critiques and iterations. My role shifts towards facilitating the learning – helping students respond to feedback, solve problems, reflect and connect their experience to curriculum outcomes.

I have found teaching this way less draining and avoided the sense of burnout I had experienced previously, while students engage with more authentic voices and expectations. These projects don’t add extra work on top of the curriculum; they become a vehicle through which the curriculum is delivered.

“The project ends. The evidence remains.”

This approach raised another question: how do we understand what students actually gain from these experiences?

That question led me to develop Pebble, an EdTech platform used at North West Regional College to support project-based and employer-engaged learning, entrepreneurship and innovation. In some ways, it works a little like a dating app for education – matching students, lecturers and external partners with the right projects and opportunities.

At the end of a project, students, lecturers and external partners evaluate the experience in around 12 minutes. Together, these perspectives provide insight into educational gain and the human, transversal and meta skills students demonstrate – including communication, collaboration, problem-solving and adaptability – increasingly important in an AI-enabled world.

The resulting learning analytics have value across the institution. They can support quality and curriculum improvement, careers and employability, employer engagement, student support and marketing – providing a wider picture of projects, student development and educational gain. External feedback can also help evidence the social value created for employers, community organisations and the communities they support. Crucially, the evidence is gathered as the learning happens. At the end of the academic year, when workloads are already high, lecturers don’t have to reconstruct what happened. Evidence is already available for self-evaluation, reporting and quality improvement, supporting a more agile approach to inspection readiness.

The project ends, but the evidence remains.

A shared responsibility

Perhaps my biggest lesson is that meaningful experience doesn’t need to sit solely on the shoulders of the lecturer. Employers bring genuine problems, professional expectations and feedback. Lecturers facilitate and connect these experiences to the curriculum. Students actively participate, while support teams benefit from the evidence generated.

This isn’t about replacing academic learning with workplace training. It is about building a stronger bridge between the two – embedding meaningful industry experience into the curriculum and creating evidence of what students actually gain from it.If meaningful industry experience is critical to graduate success, how do we ensure every student has access to it before they graduate?

title: Lived experience in teaching accessibility
summary: The post Lived experience in teaching accessibility appeared first on Advance HE UK.
full_text:
Dr Martine van Driel, SFHEA, shares her thoughts and tips on including lived experience in teaching about accessibility.

When teaching about accessibility, higher education can sometimes be overly theoretical. It is crucial that students are given opportunities to see the impact and everyday experiences of inaccessible spaces.

Inviting guest speakers with lived experience into our modules can achieve this. They bring concepts into focus, challenge assumptions and show why inclusive practice matters. By treating lived experience as a source of knowledge, students learn the importance of diverse perspectives. This blog not only outlines the value of guest speakers with lived experience but also provides practical tips on how to organise this in your teaching.

Why lived experience speakers?

While theoretical approaches to accessibility and inclusion are important and valuable to teach, they can also create a discussion of accessibility that is detached from day-to-day experiences. Considering the diversity of disabilities and the individuality of each person, (in)accessibility can look different per person and per day.

A guest speaker can share their individual experiences, demonstrating to students that this is not just theory, these are everyday experiences that affect people’s lives. That perspective can make an issue memorable in a way a definition alone may not. Additionally, hearing different perspectives encourages students to ask questions instead of assuming they already know what people need, an issue that is commonly raised in disability work (Disability by Design: Representation in TV | Bournemouth University).

As lecturers, we are experts on the theory and the academic knowledge, but we cannot be experts on everyday experiences across populations. Academic teaching offers frameworks for understanding accessibility: concepts, theories, policy and critical debate. Lived experience sits alongside this knowledge, as a way of testing how ideas meet reality. Inviting guest speakers with lived experience allows us to fill this gap in our teaching. It provides the type of knowledge and understanding that theory and academic learning alone cannot cover. The purpose is not to ask a speaker to represent an entire disability group, or to turn a personal story into a teaching resource without care. It is to make space for individual expertise and insight, while recognising that no one person can speak for everyone.

The student experience

The module I teach at the University of Birmingham focuses on inclusive digital media, and I invite guest speakers throughout the module to share their experiences both in everyday life and their use of digital media. Student feedback shows the positive impact of these sessions, with module evaluations often focusing on the guest speakers.

When asked for their favourite part of the module, students overwhelmingly listed the guest speakers. They highlighted the ease with which the speakers allowed them to grasp accessibility, and that the practical insights the speakers brought complemented the theoretical discussions in the module to expand their understanding. It also gave students access to voices and experiences that they may otherwise not have gotten in contact with and gave them a focus on the purpose of the module, allowing them to put the content into perspective.

The guest speaker sessions were recorded with consent of the speakers and made available to students via the virtual learning environment. Various students cited the guest speakers in their assignments, which was encouraged, to support their analysis with both lived experience and theoretical knowledge.

Practical tips

Careful planning matters. Invite speakers because their expertise is relevant, brief them on the session and give them a clear choice about what they do and do not wish to discuss. Also ensure that students are prepared. Share key terms, explain respectful discussion expectations and invite questions focused on learning rather than personal disclosure. After the session, let students connect what they heard to course concepts and consider whether any of their assumptions were challenged.

Here are some tips for planning such sessions:

Invite expertise, not a representative. Do not expect or ask anyone to speak on behalf of a group but rather ask them to share their expertise. Make it clear to students that guest speakers are not representatives of an entire group.

Reach out to charities centred around advocacy. Organisations such as SCOPE focus on ‘transforming attitudes’ so are a good start.

Ensure accessibility for your sessions. Check in with guest speakers about formats, communication support, venue or online arrangements and other requirements, and be ready to provide any adjustments. Do not make assumptions about what the speaker may want or need.

Agree boundaries and payment. Discuss topics, recording and reuse of materials in advance and re-confirm after the session is complete. Compensate speakers in line with institutional guidance.

Prepare students. Establish respectful ground rules, explain relevant language and encourage considered questions. Share with the students the language that the guest speaker uses to refer to themselves, so students can use that.

Make participation flexible. Offer various ways to ask questions, including polling software or advance submissions.

Reflect and follow up. Give students time to connect the session to academic ideas and ask speakers for feedback.

Lived experience speakers can transform accessibility from a topic students study into an understanding of the practical implications of inaccessible design and spaces. When contributions are planned carefully and treated as expertise, students gain a richer understanding of inclusion and a stronger basis for creating environments where more people can participate.

Dr Martine van Driel is an Assistant Professor in Digital Media & Communication at the University of Birmingham. She holds a Senior Fellowship of the Higher Education Academy. Her research focuses on autistic communication, which expands into her teaching on inclusivity and accessibility.

full_text:
At one elite California college, a student might conduct a research project this summer. At another, she’s building a product for an outside organization this summer.

At yet another, she’ll spend her summers (and the rest of the year) exploring difficult questions in a small liberal arts seminar.

This is by no means a comprehensive list of every great elite college in California, as there’s no way to be, given that different students want different things from college.

But California is lucky to offer different options for a more serious education, whether that means immersing yourself in scientific research à la Caltech or building a product for an outside organization à la Harvey Mudd. The order below is our index, and not an official ranking, since this list is not sorted by acceptance rates, or a comparison of tuitions.

“Colleges” refers both to universities and schools with a more undergraduate-centric mission. What does matter in this ranking: the depth of the education (which is weighted most heavily), opportunities for original research or other creative projects as an undergrad, and breadth.

Some smaller, more specialized colleges made this list on account of depth; larger universities can check more boxes in terms of breadth.

Each entry includes an explanation of its inclusion and some of the opportunities available to undergrads that make it special. Prestige is not the be-all-end-all, and we wanted to focus more on schools with substance, places where a student can do interesting work.

15

California Polytechnic State University, San Luis Obispo

California Polytechnic State University, San Luis Obispo (better known as Cal Poly), fits many of these criteria but is best described as being a university centered around the practical application of knowledge in higher education.

With the motto “Learn by Doing,” projects are incorporated in classes at all levels relating to concepts learned in technology, design, agriculture, the environment, etc.

Quality of education at the University is measured not only in theoretical concepts that can be committed to memory, but also in the products and issues that undergraduates study, produce, and conquer. A major differentiating factor of Cal Poly is the senior project.1

During their four years of undergraduate work leading up to a bachelor’s degree, students engage in a wide-reaching project that takes all that they have learned and condenses it into one final product.

Not only is this an impressive feat to complete, it also allows Cal Poly graduates to apply to graduate school or jobs not only armed with a great transcript, but also a final product demonstrating what they are capable of.

Although it checks most of the same boxes, an undergraduate seeking hands-on application of learning may hold Cal Poly higher than your typical liberal arts university.

14

Scripps College

One of Scripps College’s biggest strengths is its intellectually demanding yet intimate and personal liberal arts education.

Scripps’s interdisciplinary two-course Core curriculum1 immerses students in an education that encourages them to consider new sources of evidence and incites debate from the moment they enter campus.

And from this exciting beginning, Scripps nurtures students’ love of reading, writing and making connections across disciplinary boundaries, eventually resulting in strong research and writing skills developed at a startlingly early point in students’ undergraduate careers and leading ultimately to a culminating, significant piece of original research in the form of a senior thesis.1

The college also encourages double or dual majors that thoughtfully unite areas of study and interest that at first blush may appear quite different.

In our opinion, there’s simply nothing like Scripps among elite schools of higher education in California, especially for the forward-thinking and intellectually curious student who seeks an alternative to large, impersonal universities and lecture-hall-centric learning models. At Scripps, all students, not just members of some honors group, are challenged to undertake original research, produce a capstone project and build meaningful relationships with excellent faculty members in the humanities, the arts, the social and natural sciences, and everywhere in between.

13

Pitzer College

Pitzer College, a member school of The Claremont Colleges, is unique in many ways.

Interdisciplinary learning, social responsibility and environmental sustainability are just a few of the core values of Pitzer.1 They are infused into the curriculum. At Pitzer there is an emphasis on challenging the traditional boundaries among academic disciplines and creating a curriculum that reflects the student’s individual interests.

Learning starts with a first-year seminar experience,1 which introduces students to scholarship with a strong sense of community. From there, students will take, on average, 15-person classes1 where they are challenged to take ownership of their education and seek ways to apply learning to real-world situations.

This is no doubt part of what makes Pitzer’s interdisciplinary program so unique: pairing environmental issues with public policy or approaching community concerns from a humanities perspective.

Pitzer College makes it onto this list not necessarily because of the range of departments offered (since this is a smaller college and doesn’t have nearly as many majors as larger research universities), but for offering a very idiosyncratic education. Also, Pitzer students benefit from their affiliation with The Claremont Colleges; students may take courses on any of The Claremont College’s campuses,1 broadening the academic options typically available in a smaller college.

12

University of California, Davis

When choosing schools, don’t overlook UC Davis.

Especially if you’re interested in the complicated relationship of food/agriculture, environment and human survival, UC Davis should be on your list!

The College of Agricultural and Environmental Sciences is a unique and underutilized resource,1 teaching courses and encouraging research that encompasses an array of disciplines.

Agriculture and the environment don’t always fit neatly into one subject, and neither do humans. CA&ES’s curriculum reflects this and includes the social sciences alongside1 traditional agricultural and environmental courses.

AE explores the science behind the food that we eat, our dependence on food, and agriculture’s effect on the environment. Essentially, CA&ES delves into messy, real-life issues.

Which is precisely why I love CA&ES.

If this sounds like your cup of tea (or wine or kombucha…), CA&ES encourages its undergrads to get involved with research ASAP and provides useful steps to finding a faculty mentor1 and digging deeper into her/his area(s) of interest.

Many CA&ES undergrad researchers present their research at the undergraduate research conference!1 UC Davis is one of CA’s elite universities because of its dedication and commitment to find solutions to real-life problems, problems you can touch.

Get beyond school name recognition and fame, dig deeper and explore each university’s departments and areas of specialty that excite and challenge you.

11

University of California, Santa Barbara

There are actually three options at UC Santa Barbara, the College of Letters and Science, the College of Engineering, and the College of Creative Studies,1 so make sure you know the differences among these colleges before applying.

UCSB, which is consistently ranked among the best schools in California, gets much of its luster from its College of Creative Studies (CCS).

Arguably UCSB’s most interesting (and hardest to gain admission to) aspect, CCS is a small intellectual community within the larger UC Santa Barbara, a big research university with lots of resources at its students’ disposal. Note that the "creative" in CCS doesn’t refer only to creative fields, like art, music, or literature; it refers to the creation of new ideas and new bodies of work, be they in the sciences or in mathematics.

Nine majors fall under CCS,1 including physics, math, computing, marine science, and, yes, art and writing and literature.

Admission is far from automatic, as students hoping to get into CCS need to apply for admission to it specifically, so make sure CCS is right for you (an opportunity for undergraduates to dig deeply and learn as much as they can about certain fields) before applying.

10

University of California, Irvine

At UCI, students have the opportunity to dig into a research question, produce an artistic work, or explore a question of interpretation with ongoing faculty mentorship.

Mentored research is also required of students in the Campuswide Honors Collegium (two quarters minimum),1 concluding with a thesis or creative project or a paper suitable for publication.

If you’re in Campuswide Honors, mentored research is a program requirement, which provides some structure, as well as heightened expectations, beyond that offered to students who conduct mentored research outside of honors.

Mentored research is absolutely not, however, the province of honors students.

Students from all majors may undertake original creative and scholarly research.

For more information, contact your discipline department or the University Undergraduate Research Opportunities Program (UROP).1 This university program supports students of all majors who work with faculty mentors, offers advice about applications for honors that recognize or provide financial support for undergraduate research, and more.

Whatever field of endeavor you’re exploring, a project done in partnership with a faculty member may help you decide if you want to go on to graduate or professional school, or to a career in research. Faculty mentorship can be a formative part of a UCI education: it moves students beyond absorbing knowledge to creating it.

Nothing says intellectual vitality and energy quite like original work; completing even challenging courses just shows you can cross the finish line, but creating new knowledge, be it in the arts or the sciences, says that you have the confidence to embrace new challenges.

9

University of California, San Diego

If you are passionate about the ocean and natural systems in general, UC San Diego is an excellent place for you to go to school.

Not many places can boast being on the ocean like UCSD does.

Because of this, its research capabilities have been integrated into its undergraduate program, making the university highly ranked. UCSD houses the renowned Scripps Institution of Oceanography.

Scripps may not sound undergraduate-friendly (it is well-known as a center for earth and marine sciences research), but there are actually several degree options at Scripps: marine biology, geosciences, oceanic and atmospheric sciences, to name a few.1 Research opportunities for ambitious, science-oriented undergraduates abound at UCSD, ranging from joining one of a faculty member’s research teams (for credit!),1 to working directly on current research projects.

Although not all UCSD students get to participate in cutting-edge scientific research, there are certainly avenues that interested students can follow to be a part of this integral aspect of UCSD.

Being involved in research projects allows for a level of education that cannot be matched, as it allows for theory learned in classes to be applied to real, cutting-edge questions and, in a way, learning how new knowledge is actually created.

8

Claremont McKenna College

CMC is selective, combining the benefits of a smaller, liberal arts style college with excellent research opportunities.

Discussion-oriented classes and eleven different research institutes1 that tie CMC more closely to academia and larger, real-world issues have given CMC an excellent name for itself. CMC receives its ranking because the College makes intellectualism a large part of daily life on campus.

The Marian Miner Cook Athenaeum brings speakers on-campus four nights a week1 during the school year for fellow students to meet with. CMC students can come and learn about new ideas, ask questions, and discuss issues over dinner.

Student fellows moderate and host some of the events.1 This is an excellent forum for students to discuss certain issues and then, possibly, meet a guest speaker that day who studies or discusses, or has some other public affiliation with that same issue in class that week.

CMC is ideal for the student that enjoys discussion and is interested in institutions, leadership, and public issues.

These opportunities and many others on campus help students go further into their interests before heading into careers, graduate or professional schools.

7

University of Southern California

Located in Los Angeles, the University of Southern California is no slouch in size.

USC includes 23 different schools and divisions that offer a wide variety of undergraduate and graduate programs.1 With USC, you’ll have the opportunity to delve into the depths of cutting-edge neuroscience one day and creating VR worlds the next, all in the span of one sprawling campus.

USC’s rigorous, interdisciplinary programs join theory with practice, spanning from film to media to design, USC encourages exploration into the nitty-gritty of how things are made and who sees them in the end.

One of USC’s shining stars is its School of Cinematic Arts.

At the intersection of research in all moving-image media and practice in interactive technologies, USC’s School of Cinematic Arts explores the union of technology and creation with audiences in mind.1

However, even if USC as a whole might catch your eye, it’s important to do your research regarding programs or majors of particular interest to you.

Gaining acceptance into USC does not necessarily mean acceptance to certain programs/majors/upper-level classes.

Always make sure you understand the application/admission process for specific programs.

6

Harvey Mudd College

Harvey Mudd College creates a common foundation for all students in the STEM disciplines as well as an appreciation for the importance of study in the arts, humanities, and social sciences.1 Such breadth, and an awareness of the implications and consequences of technical advances and proficiency in communicating one’s ideas, are treated as goals, not just hoops to jump through in order to get a degree.

Perhaps most unique is Harvey Mudd’s Clinic Program in which teams of 4-5 students undertake major projects in engineering, CS, math, or physics.1

These projects are defined in collaboration with outside organizations and focus on real world problems and applications not generally encountered in the normal curriculum.

Such projects force the participating students to work closely together and define much of the work for themselves.

All of this leads to a rigorous and interdisciplinary education which explains how Harvey Mudd ranks above several much larger universities. Harvey Mudd may offer a smaller range of disciplines but it wins hands down in focus on undergraduate education and quality.

For a student wishing to pursue a technical field the combination of breadth, teamwork and real projects is incredibly appealing.

5

Pomona College

Pomona College in Claremont, California is one of the most elite schools in California. Pomona’s high ranking is due in part to the school’s excellent undergraduate/faculty relationship.

Students receive outstanding mentoring and opportunities for discussion and feedback with professors, rather than simply passively sitting through lectures.

Pomona College offers students access to other nearby schools’ academic resources, which expands the educational and intellectual opportunities students have to participate in.

Pomona College is focused only on undergraduates.

The School offers its students a Summer Undergraduate Research Program that funds research with faculty, as well as student-initiated research.1

This gives students who aren’t sure they want to go on to graduate school, or simply aren’t interested in their field of study, enough time to explore other fields and piques student interest to think independently.

Being a part of The Claremont Colleges is a plus for Pomona. Access to other institutions in the consortium means increased resources for Pomona, and broader subject-matter offerings.

Depending on the major and certain regulations and advising, Pomona College allows its students the ability to cross-register at another Claremont School.1 They suggest careful consideration and intentional planning before taking a core class for one’s major at another institution.

4

University of California, Los Angeles

UCLA is a large public research university, and undergraduates can capitalize on the research opportunities available to them.

Check out UCLA’s research portal,1 projects led by faculty members and resources to help find a mentor on the university’s undergraduate admission website! UCLA has programs available to undergraduate students in all areas of humanities, the life and physical sciences, the social sciences, and in the specialized schools.

If you peruse UCLA’s major listings you’ll see a long, long list of possible paths1 you could take during your undergraduate education.

UCLA is near the top of the list for breadth of education one can receive all from a single university.

However, this breadth of opportunities will be of little significance to you unless you make it relevant by learning more about what faculty are doing in their research, by asking questions, connecting dots between interests, etc. Maybe you start out interested in a particular discipline only to find out there are related fields.

Narrow in on what interests you the most and create your own niche combining classes and research projects.

Going to classes and leaving it at that won’t create an educational experience.

Speak to professors, challenge yourself and find opportunities; you’ll be surprised with all that can be done.

Chart your own path, for your education is your creation.

3

University of California, Berkeley

Whether students want to explore problems through the lens of scientific evidence, history, public policy or design, there’s a UC Berkeley major for that, ranging from arts and humanities to engineering1 and many specialties in between. UC Berkeley has plenty of research programs on campus, including the Undergraduate Research Apprentice Program,1 as well as a variety of faculty-led opportunities available for interested undergrads.

Being mentored by professors and made a part of an academic community can only help students down the line, and allows them to start making professional connections early in their college careers. It comes as no surprise that our countdown includes a couple of large, public universities, and UC Berkeley outshines many smaller institutions because of the sheer number of incredible programs the school offers in a variety of fields.

Overall, your experience as a UC Berkeley undergrad will be what you make of it, involving the classes you take, the faculty mentor you work with, and the research projects you’re a part of.

Students who are eager to participate in their education, think critically about issues and seek out opportunities will make the most of what this school has to offer. If you’re the type to stray beyond the lecture halls, this is the place for you!

2

California Institute of Technology

Caltech, located in Pasadena, also has a strong curriculum that focuses on both rigor and balance. All Caltech students are expected to take rigorous science and math classes.

In addition, Caltech requires humanities and social sciences classes1 that are relevant to students’ fields so that they learn not only how to tackle complex issues but how to communicate these issues in an understandable way. Caltech also offers students the opportunity to participate in their Summer Undergraduate Research Fellowships.

Caltech students work with a mentor to design a project and submit a proposal defending this project. Chosen students then conduct research for the ten weeks of summer culminating in a technical paper and an oral presentation.1

This is an amazing program because it allows undergraduate students an opportunity for hands-on experience.

There is only so much that can be taught in the classroom; by participating in the program, students see what research is really like, learning to formulate a question and defend the importance of exploring this question, conducting research, and disseminating results. It is this well-thought-out curriculum and hands-on experiences in science, math, or engineering research that make Caltech so rigorous and focused.

This intensity contributes to the university’s #2 rank.

1

Stanford University

At Stanford University you’ll find programs of study and research in the humanities, in the sciences and in engineering; programs dedicated to sustainability; programs for studying away; programs for working closely with a professor on research. Roughly a third of Stanford undergraduates receive funding to undertake such projects1 (through grants from the Office of the Vice Provost for Undergraduate Education), working beyond the call of classroom lecture on topics of their own intellectual curiosity, and there is a reason this university takes top honors in our reckoning, as there’s nowhere else like it, both so broad and so deep in its undergraduate offerings.

It’s a research environment second to none: with over 7,500 externally sponsored research projects on Stanford’s campus and 20 Nobel laureates among its researchers,1 it’s little wonder that Stanford undergrads can immerse themselves so completely in their areas of study. Though they focus on their major, as undergraduates Stanford students will have a chance to explore deeply an impressive number of subject matters.

title: Milano entra nel futuro: al via la Zis sull’Intelligenza Artificiale
summary:
Computer vision per ridurre gli scarti. E poi estrazione documentale rapida da fonti eterogenee, condivisione dei dati lungo la supply chain, realizzazione facilitata di preventivi tecnici per capitolati complessi.

full_text:
«Se vogliamo continuare ad essere competitivi nel mondo - sintetizza il presidente dell’Ice Matteo Zoppas - c’è un solo treno che sta passando, quello dell’intelligenza artificiale, treno che dobbiamo prendere ora. Utilizzando i nuovi strumenti per cogliere nuove opportunità, amplificando la creatività del Made in Italy». Pilastro principale della strategia è lo sfruttamento dei punti di forza del nostro sistema industriale. Perché se dal lato degli sviluppi in termini di modelli e piattaforme la supremazia di Usa e in seconda battuta Cina è evidente, è nell’applicazione concreta di queste metodiche che l’Italia può giocare un ruolo di primo piano.

La capacità manifatturiera integrata con una nuova intelligenza - questa la scommessa - può diventare così un asset formidabile per rilanciare il nostro ruolo sui mercati globali e attrarre investimenti che guardino all’Italia come piattaforma produttiva evoluta. Obiettivi raggiungibili se le nostre aziende saranno in grado di attraversare il guado: passando dall’AI generativa a quella integrata nei processi decisionali e operativi. «Il vantaggio italiano - aggiunge il presidente di Made Competence center Marco Taisch – non è l’algoritmo ma il saper fare. È in questo passaggio dal progetto pilota all’industrializzazione che Made metterà a disposizione della nuova Zis la propria esperienza. Partendo da ciò che sappiamo fare: dalla nostra fabbrica dimostrativa, dove le aziende possono vedere in azione le tecnologie prima ancora di investire; dagli ambienti di sperimentazione protetti, dai percorsi di formazione costruiti sui fabbisogni delle imprese». Nell’evento di ieri, svolto in Assolombarda, protagoniste sono state proprio le imprese, italiane e non solo, realtà (si vedano articoli a lato in pagina) che hanno esposto le esperienze di Physical AI sviluppate: tra robot saldatori e consegne hi tech dell’ultimo miglio, linee robotizzate per biofarmaci, droni in grado di mappare i progressi di un cantiere. Non un futuro possibile, ma uno spicchio già ben visibile di “presente”. «La Physical AI - conclude Biffi - è centrale per la nostra industria e sviluppando questo asset possiamo attrarre capitali e talenti: perché i giovani, in genere, decidono di andare là dove si crea il futuro».

Le storie d’impresa/1: Fincantieri

Anche in un settore in apparenza maturo, come quello della cantieristica navale, la Physical AI entra nei processi quotidiani, come testimonia l’esperienza di Fincantieri, che al tema dell’automazione avanzata e dell’innovazione industriale ha dedicato un piano ad hoc (Boost) da 100 milioni e un centro di eccellenza da 20 persone. Le esperienze operative, in cui l’AI entra in gioco, in primis nella fase di apprendimento delle macchine, vedono ad esempio i robot utilizzati per verificare lo stato di avanzamento dei cantieri, mappando e segnalando le modifiche di ogni punto della nave rispetto alla rilevazione precedente, schema già operativo nel sito di Monfalcone. Vi sono poi rover che in autonomia trasportano il materiale nei siti e droni che tramite computer vision verificano i giunti di saldature. Attività che già ora sono realizzate utilizzando Cobot e in prospettiva (primi test a Sestri Levante nel 2027) umanoidi.

«L’Ai - spiega l’ad e direttore generale di Fincantieri Pierroberto Folgiero - è una leva chiave per la trasformazione della cantieristica e per la competitività della nostra industria. Portarla nel mondo fisico significa accompagnare l’evoluzione dei processi industriali attraverso una sempre maggiore integrazione tra tecnologia, robotica e competenze. È un percorso che aumenta la produttività, migliora l’efficienza e valorizza il know-how industriale, rafforzando la capacità della manifattura di affrontare le sfide di un contesto in continua evoluzione».

Le storie d’impresa/2: Coco Robotics

Non in un garage, questa volta ma in uno studentato. Poco cambia tuttavia, perché il percorso avviato dal basso di Coco Robotics conferma la vitalità del sistema di start up made in Usa, dove l’idea spesso riesce a scalare verso l’alto in modo rapido. Realtà fondata sei anni fa in California da Zach Rash e Brad Squicciarini, all’epoca due neolaureati della Ucla appassionati di tecnologia per la guida autonoma.

Loading...

L’idea di partenza, poi realizzata, era quella di creare un mini-veicolo elettrico compatto, specializzato esclusivamente nel trasporto di piccoli ordini per il cosiddetto “ultimo miglio”.

Espansione che procede anche oltre gli Stati Uniti, come testimoniato dall’accordo raggiunto con Deliveroo per portare le consegne con robot in città e centri abitati di tutto il Regno Unito (si parte a Londra da Canary Wharf). Progetti che si alimentano grazie agli 80 milioni di dollari raccolti in estate dagli investitori: così , dalle 50 marche gestite in consegna due anni fa, l’azienda è salita ora a quota cinquemila. L’intelligenza artificiale entra in gioco per ottenere un posizionamento Gps corretto anche nelle situazioni cittadine più complesse mentre le reti neurali elaborano in tempo reale i dati dei sensori Lidar e a ultrasuoni, così come delle telecamere ad alta risoluzione, riducendo al minimo l’intervento degli operatori da remoto e rilevando in modo istantaneo ostacoli e pedoni.

L’azienda è in forte crescita e dal suo avvio ha già effettuato più di 500 mila consegne a emissioni zero.

Le storie d’impresa/3: Multiply Labs

Quattro persone ora. Che saliranno a 20 già il prossimo anno, per arrivare a quasi 50 quello successivo. Crescita attesa rilevante quella della branch italiana di Multiply Labs, start up californiana impegnata nel realizzare sistemi robotici per terapie biologiche avanzate. L’idea, già sviluppata in applicazioni concrete, è quella di sostituire il più possibile la manipolazione umana dei materiali, eliminando i rischi di contaminazione e aumentando in modo esponenziale la produttività. «In questo modo - spiega il Chief manufacturing officer di Multiply Labs, Enrico Racca - i costi di queste cure, che per una singola persona possono arrivare a 300mila dollari, si abbattono drasticamente aumentandone l’accessibilità. In termini di produttività al metro quadro si può crescere di due ordini di grandezza». Passando da uno schema con 4-8 operatori che nell’unità di tempo realizzano 1-2 dosi in 100 metri quadri a un altro in cui un solo operatore, nella metà dello spazio, può arrivare a produrre decine di terapie. Risultati raggiunti replicando i processi produttivi e la manipolazione delle cellule effettuata dai tecnici con sistemi robotici e applicando la Physical AI. «Questo - spiega il manager - ci consente di utilizzare i video girati all’interno delle camere bianche per insegnare ai robot i movimenti e le procedure esatte da effettuare, determinanti per la buona riuscita del processo». Sul mercato Multiply Labs ha già alcune applicazioni concrete presso case farmaceutiche, con l’Italia a giocare un ruolo chiave nella messa a terra manifatturiera dell’intero processo.

title: Formazione AI nelle PMI: i fondi ci sono, ma restano inutilizzati
summary:
Le PMI versano ogni anno risorse ai fondi interprofessionali, ma spesso ignorano di poterle recuperare per finanziare corsi sull’intelligenza artificiale. Tra adesioni dimenticate, scarsa informazione e procedure affidate agli intermediari, le imprese più piccole restano escluse proprio quando cresce il bisogno di alfabetizzazione AI
